sources.entry: Depflush - Finds what Docker, node_modules, old IDEs and duplicate files leave behind, with a preview and the Trash by default.

summary.one_liner: Depflush is a free macOS app that scans for leftover developer files (Docker leftovers, node_modules and vendor folders, duplicate files, SQL dumps, and caches) and lets you preview and remove them, with the Trash as the default.
summary.what_it_does: It lists each candidate item with its size before anything is moved. Docker: build cache and unused re-pullable images are preselected, while locally built images, stopped containers and orphaned volumes are flagged and never preselected. Dependencies: vendor/ folders next to composer.lock and node_modules/ next to package.json in projects untouched for 12 months (configurable). Duplicates: photos and videos in common user folders are compared by size, then partial bytes, then SHA-256, keeping one original. SQL dumps over 100 MB are deduplicated by SHA-256. Caches: 30+ locations including browsers, editors, package managers and old JetBrains IDE versions. A menu bar item shows free space and warns when it drops below a threshold.
use_cases: free up disk space on a Mac used for development
remove unused Docker images and build cache
delete old node_modules and vendor folders from inactive projects
find and remove duplicate photos and videos
clear package manager and IDE caches
review cleanup items before deleting them
how_to_run: Or download Depflush.zip from the latest GitHub release, unzip, and move Depflush to Applications
notable: Preview-and-confirm workflow; nothing is deleted without confirmation, and the Trash is the default destination
Risky items such as Docker volumes, containers, locally built images and plugin dependencies are never preselected
Duplicate detection goes size, then first/last bytes, then SHA-256, and never scans the Photos library, app bundles or iCloud placeholders
No Xcode project or external dependencies; built with a shell script
No network calls, analytics or account required
caveats: Not notarized by Apple yet, so first launch requires approving it in System Settings → Privacy & Security
Releases are signed and published by the maintainer; building from source is the alternative
